source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part III 2007: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/julio_07/09072007_01.asp); Philip II Relaciones Topograficas 1575; Leon Pinelo Anales de Madrid; Sanchez Gonzalez 'De Alarnes a Getafe' (Ayto. Getafe 1989); Jimenez de Gregorio; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xatafi

name: Getafe Sector 3
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Sector 3' neighbourhood of Getafe, a planned residential development. Opened 1995.

name: Las Margaritas Universidad
etymology_summary: 'Las Margaritas' is a 1960s neighbourhood in Getafe with flower-themed street names (Lilas, Loto, Camelias). 'Universidad' refers to Carlos III University campus nearby.
named_after: Las Margaritas neighbourhood + Universidad Carlos III

name: El Casar
etymology_summary: Named after the El Casar area of Getafe Norte. 'Casar' derives from Latin 'casale' meaning a group of houses or a hamlet.
named_after: El Casar (from casar: group of houses/hamlet)

name: Pinto
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007) favours Latin 'pinctus' (painted/of a certain colour), an adjective describing terrain coloration where the original noun (mons, campus, etc.) was lost. The phonetic evolution pinctus > Pinto is regular (cf. sanctum > santo). The popular theory from Latin 'punctum' (point/crossing) is phonetically problematic: punctum should yield 'Punto', not 'Pinto'. A folk legend ('La Leyenda del Arca') claims Pinto marks the geographic centre of the Iberian Peninsula. The anthroponym Pintus (personal name) is also possible but unsubstantiated.
named_after: Pinto (from Latin pinctus: painted/coloured, per Garcia Sanchez)
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007); Ayto. Pinto; Wikipedia

name: Valdemoro
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. The Toponomasticon Hispaniae (Nieto Ballester, UAM) favours Latin VALLE + MAURA/MAURU meaning 'dark/dusky valley', describing dark terrain: Vallemoro > Valmoro > Valdemoro. Documented as 'Vallem Maurii' under Alfonso VIII. Alternative theories: (1) 'Valley of the Moor(s)' from Reconquista context; (2) Arabic 'Wadi al-murr' (bitter river); (3) 'valley of blackberries' (Latin morum); (4) personal name Maurus; (5) Latin *murus* (wall/ruin) indicating collapsed structures during repopulation (per Historia de Valdemoro blog); (6) 'val de moras' (mulberry valley, per Pancracio Celdran). Garcia Sanchez discusses the name in CVC Rinconete Part IV (2008).
named_after: Valle moro (dark valley, per Toponomasticon Hispaniae)
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae (toponhisp.org/es/toponimia-de-las-zonas-central-sur-e-insular-atlantica/toponimo/valdemoro); Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2008: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/enero_08/28012008_01.htm); Galmes de Fuentes; historiadevaldemoro.blogspot.com/2016/10/toponimia.html; Alfonso X docs 1274; Primera Cronica c.1270-1290

name: Ciempozuelos
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'cien pozuelos' (a hundred small wells), where 'cien' is not literal but means 'many'. A spring at Buzanca (c.2 km away) fed a canal to the town fountain, but since the flow was insufficient, numerous wells were dug to supplement the water supply. The many wells gave the town its name.

name: Aranjuez
etymology_summary: Named after the royal town. Most accepted etymology: Basque origin from 'arantza' (thorn/hawthorn), per Rafael Lapesa. Medieval forms -- Aranz/Arauz (12th c.), Aranzuel (13th c.), Aranjuez (15th c.) -- show progressive suffixation consistent with a Basque base. Fray Martin Sarmiento (18th c.) proposed Latin 'Ara Jovis' (altar of Jupiter); Roman artifacts found in the area but no altar recovered. Terminus of Spain's first railway (1851).
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part I: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/junio_07/06062007_01.htm); Rafael Lapesa; Fray Martin Sarmiento; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aranjuez_(Madrid); CVC Cervantes

name: Parla
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Most accepted theory (Garcia Sanchez, CVC): derives from Roman anthroponym 'Parilus', designating the property owner's estate: Latin (villa) Parila > Parla. Alternative: Latin 'palus' (lagoon/swamp), proposed by Jimenez Gregorio, plausible given the sandy soil producing seasonal lagoons. The folk etymology about a mute woman who began to 'parlar' (speak) after drinking from a fountain is legend.
named_after: Parla (from Roman anthroponym Parilus, per Garcia Sanchez)
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete); Fernando Jimenez Gregorio; Wikipedia

name: Fuencarral
etymology_summary: Named after the old town of Fuencarral, annexed to Madrid. From 'Fuente Carral' -- a spring (fuente) where carts (carros) stopped and animals drank. The stopping place for carts was called a 'carra', hence 'Fuente carra' > 'Fuencarral'. The spring was known as 'Fuente del Concejo' on the old road to Alcobendas.
named_after: Fuencarral (Fuente Carral: spring where carts stopped)
source: El Rincon de Mayrit; Wikipedia; Vena Madrid

name: Cantoblanco Universidad
etymology_summary: 'Cantoblanco' likely means 'white rock/edge' (from 'canto' = stone/edge + 'blanco' = white), describing the terrain. 'Universidad' refers to the Universidad Autonoma de Madrid campus located here since 1970.
named_after: Cantoblanco (white boulder) + Universidad Autonoma de Madrid

name: Alcobendas-San Sebastian de los Reyes
etymology_summary: Alcobendas: Menendez Pidal proposed pre-Roman 'Alcovindos' (hill); Villar Liebana suggests 'Alcebindos' (hill of the roe deer). First documented in the Fuero de Madrid (1202) as 'Alcovendas'. Alternatives: Arabic 'al-kubun' (dome/house) or hybrid 'al-' + 'so-' + 'Vendas' (beneath the inns). San Sebastian de los Reyes: named after the patron saint and the Catholic Monarchs (Reyes Catolicos) who granted its charter.
named_after: Alcobendas (possibly pre-Roman: hill) + San Sebastian de los Reyes
source: Menendez Pidal; Villar Liebana; CVC Cervantes; Moncloa.com; MadridNorte24h

name: El Goloso
etymology_summary: Named after the El Goloso neighbourhood, which itself is named after the military base established there in the early 20th century.
named_after: El Goloso (military base/area in Tres Cantos)

name: Colmenar Viejo
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Colmenar' = place of beehives (from colmena, possibly Celtic kolmena from kolmos: straw, per Coromines). 'Viejo' = old. Per Felipe II's Relaciones Topograficas (1579), the original settlement formed around a beekeeper's house on the road between Alcala de Henares and Segovia. First documented as 'Colmenar Biejo' in 1287.
named_after: Colmenar Viejo (old beehive place, from Celtic kolmena)
source: Telemadrid; Toponomasticon Hispaniae; Ayuntamiento de Colmenar Viejo; Felipe II Relaciones 1579

name: Asamblea de Madrid-Entrevias
etymology_summary: Originally named 'Entrevias' (1977), meaning 'between the tracks', as the neighbourhood is surrounded by railway lines. Renamed in 1998 when the Asamblea de Madrid (regional parliament) building opened nearby.
named_after: Asamblea de Madrid (regional parliament) + Entrevias neighbourhood (between railway lines)

name: El Pozo
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Pozo del Tio Raimundo' neighbourhood. According to tradition, a farmer named Raimundo built a well ('pozo') and watering trough for passing livestock.
named_after: El Pozo del Tio Raimundo (neighbourhood, from pozo: well)

name: Santa Eugenia
etymology_summary: Named after the Santa Eugenia neighbourhood (1970s planned development). Streets are named after towns in Burgos province, reflecting the origin of the developers. The saint's name was likely chosen arbitrarily for the development.
named_after: Santa Eugenia neighbourhood (patron saint Eugenia of Rome)

name: Coslada
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Menendez Pidal (Toponimia Prerromanica Hispana 1952) proposed Celtic origin: 'coslo/cosla' (hazelnut) with Romance suffix '-ada', yielding 'hazelnut grove'. He cites parallels: Villa Coslus and Villa Cosla (9th-10th c. France, Marne), Coslumnus (modern Coulo, Yonne), German Kusel (Mainz). Alternative: Latin 'cos' (flint) + 'late' (extensive), from abundant gypsum/flint quarries (per Aurelio Garcia Lopez). The theory 'cova ustulata' (burnt cave) is explicitly dismissed as 'mere hypothesis' by Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2008). In his 2010 De Gruyter chapter, Garcia Sanchez calls even the Celtic theory 'mas discutible' (more debatable). First documented 1083 under Alfonso VI; earliest confirmed written mention between 1152-1273 per Julio Gonzalez (1975).
named_after: Coslada (Celtic cosla: hazelnut grove, per Menendez Pidal)
source: Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromanica Hispana (Gredos 1952); Garcia Lopez et al. 'Coslada' (Lunwerg 1998); Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2008: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/enero_08/28012008_01.htm); Garcia Sanchez 'En torno a la toponimia madrilena' (De Gruyter 2010: academia.edu/10965316); Cosladaweb

name: San Fernando
etymology_summary: Named after San Fernando de Henares. The municipality was named in honour of King Fernando VI, who developed a royal textile factory there from 1746. 'De Henares' refers to the nearby river.

name: Torrejon de Ardoz
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Torrejon' from Latin 'turris' (tower) with diminutive suffix, referring to a small medieval watchtower on the Reconquista frontier between Christian and Muslim territories (11th century). 'Ardoz' is a hydronym from the Arroyo Ardoz stream; its etymology is uncertain but has parallels with Hispano-Pyrenean toponyms (Arduix, Ardos).
named_after: Torrejon de Ardoz (medieval watchtower + Arroyo Ardoz stream)
source: Quadernillos; Toponomasticon Hispaniae; Torrejon Todo Noticias

name: Soto del Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the residential neighbourhood built along the Henares river. 'Soto' means a wooded riverside area or grove, common in Castilian toponymy.
named_after: Soto del Henares (riverside grove on the Henares river)

name: La Garena
etymology_summary: Named after the La Garena residential neighbourhood in Alcala de Henares. Carlos de Lucena (converso family) purchased a property called 'La Garena' or 'La Garcena' c.1495, which became the 'Senorio de la Garena'. The Lucena estate later became a meeting place for alumbrados (illuminists). The most plausible etymology connects it to Old French 'garenne/guarenne' (game park/rabbit warren, from Medieval Latin *warenna of Germanic origin). The variant spelling 'La Garcena' in the 1495 document may be an intermediate form. The English word 'warren' derives from the same root.
source: Diago Hernando 'El protonotario Lucena en su entorno sociopolitico' (Sefarad 53(2) 1993: sefarad.revistas.csic.es); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chorrillo-Garena; Reymundo Tornero 'Datos historicos de Alcala de Henares' (1950) p.818; etymonline.com/word/warren

name: Alcala de Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the city. 'Alcala' from Arabic 'al-qal'a' (the fortress/castle). The Muslims built a defensive enclave called 'Al-Qal'at Nahar' (the castle on the Henares). The Roman name was Complutum (confluence). 'De Henares' from the river, possibly from Latin 'foenarius' or Arabic 'en-Nahr' (the river). The Arabic 'qal'at' root is extremely productive in Iberian toponymy: Calatrava, Alcala de Guadaira, etc.
named_after: Alcala de Henares (Arabic al-qal'a: the fortress, on the Henares)
source: Etimologias de Chile; La Calle Mayor; El Complutense

name: Alcala de Henares Universidad
etymology_summary: Named for proximity to the historic University of Alcala, founded by Cardinal Cisneros in 1499. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.

name: Meco
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Etymology debated with no scholarly consensus: (1) Celtic 'miccon' (sheep) from a Celtiberian settlement; (2) Arabic 'maksusk' (bare mountain), supported by Islamic-period archaeological remains at the site; (3) RAE defines 'meco' as 'blackish-red colour', potentially a terrain descriptor. The popular identification with Roman mansio 'Miacum' from the Antonine Itinerary is rejected by modern archaeology: Rodriguez Morales and Jimenez Guijarro have identified Miacum with Collado Mediano (El Beneficio archaeological site), not Meco.
named_after: Meco (disputed: Celtic, Roman, or Arabic origin)
source: Quadernillos (quadernillos.com/el-origen-del-nombre-de-torrejon-meco-daganzo-y-camarma); Rodriguez Morales on Miacum (academia.edu); RAE (dle.rae.es/meco); Felipe II Relaciones 1579; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meco_(Madrid); amiaire.net/espana/comunidaddemadrid/cuencamediadeljarama/meco

name: Azuqueca
etymology_summary: Named after Azuqueca de Henares. From Arabic 'sukayqa' (diminutive of suq, 'little road/alley'), referring to a small path around which the first buildings were constructed.
named_after: Azuqueca de Henares (possibly Arabic al-suqayqa: small market)

name: Guadalajara
etymology_summary: Named after the city. From Arabic 'wad al-hayara' (valley of stones). The Arab city was founded 8th-9th century as 'madinat al-Faray' on the banks of the 'wad al-hayara' (the Henares river).
named_after: Guadalajara (Arabic Wadi al-Hayara: river/valley of stones)

name: Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after the Aluche neighbourhood. The name derives from the Arroyo de Luche stream, a tributary of the Manzanares. Maps noted it as 'A. Luche' (Arroyo Luche), which evolved into 'Aluche'. Documented as 'Aluche' in a Real Cedula of Felipe II (1580). Alternative theory: from Leonese wrestling ('luches') brought by immigrants.
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arroyo_Luche; telemadrid.es (Aluche el barrio que surgio de un arroyo 2023); avaaluche.wordpress.com/2020/02/04/historia-de-aluche; Real Cedula Felipe II 1580; madripedia.wikis.cc/wiki/Barrio_de_Aluche

name: Maestra Justa Freire-Polideportivo Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after Justa Freire Mendez (1896-1965), innovative pedagogue and teacher. She pioneered progressive education methods in Madrid's working-class neighbourhoods. 'Polideportivo Aluche' refers to the adjacent sports complex.

name: Las Aguilas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Aguilas neighbourhood in the Latina district. The name likely refers to eagles that once inhabited the area or to the heraldic imagery associated with local estates.

name: Cuatro Vientos
etymology_summary: Named after the Cuatro Vientos area. The toponym ('Four Winds') predates the aerodrome and refers to this open, elevated plain where winds blow from all four cardinal directions. In 1911 the lands were acquired for Spain's first military aerodrome, birthplace of Spanish aviation.

name: Laguna
etymology_summary: Named after the Laguna neighbourhood. 'Laguna' means 'lagoon' or 'small lake', suggesting historical presence of a body of standing water in the area.
named_after: Laguna neighbourhood (Latina district, from laguna: lagoon/pond)

name: Alcorcon
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007) favours a hybrid Latin+Arabic formation: the al- prefix is not the Arabic article in its original function but a superstrate adoption over a Latin root *corcu/qorq from Latin 'quercus' (oak), parallel to 'alcornoque' (cork oak). The toponym would mean 'the oak grove' as a Mozarabic hybrid. Alternative: pure Arabic 'al-kur'/'al-gor' (hill/mound), supported by local tradition and the town's elevated position. The folk etymology connecting it to Alcorcon's famous pottery tradition (via 'alcor' as copper oxide glaze) is linguistically dubious: Corominas traces 'alcorque' to Latin 'cortex' (bark), not 'quercus'. First documented 1208 as 'Canada de Alcorcon' under Alfonso VIII.
named_after: Alcorcon (hybrid al- + Latin quercus: oak grove, per Garcia Sanchez)
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007); Corominas; Ayuntamiento de Alcorcon; Alcorconhoy

name: San Jose de Valderas
etymology_summary: Named after the San Jose de Valderas neighbourhood of Alcorcon. 'San Jose' is St. Joseph; 'Valderas' likely from 'valle de eras' (valley of threshing floors). Station had origins on the old narrow-gauge Madrid-Almorox line.
named_after: San Jose de Valderas neighbourhood (patron saint + Valderas estate)

name: Las Retamas
etymology_summary: Named after the avenue and the abundant retama (broom plant, Retama sphaerocarpa) bushes in the area. 'Retama' is from Arabic 'ratama'.
named_after: Las Retamas neighbourhood (Mostoles, from retama: broom plant)

name: Mostoles
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Latin 'monisterium/monisteriis' (monasteries): Monisterium > Monsteriu > Moster > Mostel > Mosteles > Mostoles, indicating pre-Islamic Christian monasteries in the area. First document mentioning the town (1144) calls it 'Turrem de Monsteles' (Tower of Mosteles).
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part IV: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/agosto_07/31082007_02.htm); Rodriguez Morales (celtiberia.net/es/biblioteca/?id=1935); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B3stoles

name: Mostoles-El Soto
etymology_summary: 'Mostoles' - see above. 'El Soto' means 'the grove', referring to a wooded riverside area. Combined name indicates the station serves the southern/river side of Mostoles.
named_after: Mostoles + El Soto (riverside grove, from Latin saltus)

name: Leganes
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Latin 'leganos' (place with much mud/silt). Per Felipe II's 16th-century Relaciones Topograficas, the area had a lagoon with abundant 'legamo' (silt/mud). The original name was reportedly 'Legamar', later corrupted. Alternative: from 'lebanes' (person from Liebana, Cantabria). Founded c.1280 under Alfonso X; first documented 1232.
source: Secretos de Leganes; Toponomasticon Hispaniae; CVC Cervantes

name: Parque Polvoranca
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Polvoranca regional park in Leganes. 'Polvoranca' likely relates to 'polvo' (dust) or refers to an old gunpowder factory or dust-producing terrain.
named_after: Parque de Polvoranca (regional park in Leganes)

name: Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Contraction of 'Fuente Labrada' (carved/hewn fountain). Per the municipal archive and Felipe II's Relaciones Topograficas, near the village stood an old stone fountain 'labrada a cal y canto' (built of stone and mortar), believed to have been made by the Moors. The settlement took its name from this fountain.
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae; Ayuntamiento de Fuenlabrada; Memorias de Fuenlabrada

name: La Serna-Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: 'La Serna' derives from Latin 'senara' (sown field), a term used in medieval Castile for cultivated land. 'Fuenlabrada' added to indicate the municipality.
named_after: La Serna (from Latin serna: cultivated strip of land)

name: Humanes
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Humanes de Madrid. Per linguist Edelmiro Bascuas, from the Paleo-European hydronymical root *um- (from Indo-European *am-: watercourse/channel). Alternative: Latin 'humidus' (humid). Both theories converge on a water connection, consistent with the geography: a sandy plain between the Guadarrama and Jarama basins crossed by streams.
source: Bascuas, Hidronimia y lexico de origen paleoeuropeo en Galicia, 2006, p. 234; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanes_de_Madrid; Ayuntamiento de Humanes (ayto-humanesdemadrid.es)

name: Aravaca
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood of Aravaca. Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004, pp. 821-830) argues it is an ethnic designation from the Celtiberian people the Arevaci/Aravaci, not an agricultural reference. Pliny wrote 'Arevacis nomen dedit flumen Areva' (N.h. 3, 27). St. Jerome confirms Arevacan groups settled as far as Carpetanian territory. Roman cavalry units of Arevacan horsemen ('Aravacorum') are documented in CIL III 3271. Alternative: Isabel Gea's 'Ara Val Cea' (valley of Cea). The folk etymology 'ara, vaca!' (plough, cow!) from Felipe II's 1575 Relaciones lacks linguistic support. First documented in 1202 Fuero de Madrid as Sexmo de Aravaca; current form 1427.
named_after: Aravaca (ethnic designation from Celtiberian Arevaci, per Caridad Arias)
source: Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004, pp. 821-830: dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); Pliny N.h. 3, 27; Isabel Gea, Curiosidades y anecdotas de Madrid; Relaciones topograficas Felipe II 1575; Fuero de Madrid 1202

name: El Barrial-Centro Comercial Pozuelo
etymology_summary: Originally named 'El Barrial' after the neighbourhood. 'Barrial' means a muddy/clay area. Later 'Centro Comercial Pozuelo' was added after the nearby Hipercor shopping centre opened.
named_after: El Barrial area + Centro Comercial Pozuelo

name: Pozuelo
etymology_summary: Named after Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Pozuelo' from Latin 'puteolu' (diminutive of puteus: well), meaning 'place with wells/springs'. Wells reportedly dug by Muslims to supply the village. Originally 'Pozuelo de Aravaca'; renamed in 1632 when Gabriel de Ocana y Alarcon purchased the town and required his surname be added. First documented 1208.
named_after: Pozuelo de Alarcon (Latin puteolu: small well/spring)
source: Ayuntamiento de Pozuelo; Toponomasticon Hispaniae; MadridNorte24h

name: Majadahonda
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'majada' (Latin maculata: stained, a sheepfold where ground was stained by animal dung) + 'honda' (deep/low-lying terrain). Segovian shepherds settled the area in the 13th century and established their pens in a deep hollow, giving rise to the name.

name: Las Rozas
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Castilian 'roza' (land cleared for cultivation by slash-and-burn). The settlement originated as a zone of newly cleared croplands, contrasting with neighboring Majadahonda (founded by shepherds). True growth occurred in the 16th century with Madrid as capital and El Escorial's construction driving demand for agricultural areas.
named_after: Las Rozas (rozas: slash-and-burn clearings for farmland)

name: Pinar
etymology_summary: Named after 'Pinar de las Rozas' (Pine Grove of Las Rozas). Refers to the pine forest area in the municipality of Las Rozas. Full name is Pinar de las Rozas.
named_after: Pinar de las Rozas (pine grove area)

name: Las Matas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Matas neighbourhood of Las Rozas. 'Matas' means 'bushes' or 'shrubland', describing the natural vegetation of the area.

name: Torrelodones
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'Torre' (tower) + 'Lodones' (hackberry/nettle trees, Celtis australis). Refers to the medieval Andalusi watchtower (10th century), part of the Muslim defensive system, surrounded by lodon trees. Originally 'Torre de Lodones', contracted to 'Torrelodones'. First documented 1287.
source: Ayuntamiento de Torrelodones; Toponomasticon Hispaniae; MadridNorte24h

name: Galapagar-La Navata
etymology_summary: Galapagar: from 'galapago' (freshwater terrapin) + '-ar' (place abundant in). First settlements were around a small lagoon with a colony of terrapins. The municipal coat of arms features these animals. Registered in DRAE since 1899. La Navata: from 'nava' (Basque: flat land with pasture between mountains) with diminutive suffix.
named_after: Galapagar (place of terrapins) + La Navata (small pasture plain)

name: San Yago
etymology_summary: Named after a local area in Galapagar. 'San Yago' is an archaic form of 'Santiago' (Saint James), the patron saint of Spain. Reflects medieval pilgrimage traditions.
named_after: San Yago (archaic form of Santiago, patron saint: Saint James)

name: El Escorial
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Two major theories: (1) Latin 'scoria' (slag/waste), proposed by Father Siguenza (16th c.), who noted ashes and slag around the site. (2) Latin 'esculus' (oak/holm oak), proposed by Sarmiento (18th c.): 'esculealis' > 'escurial' > 'escorial'. Recent research by Auberson supports the oak theory, citing geologist Casiano de Prado's 1864 survey finding no slag deposits but documenting dense former forest cover.
named_after: El Escorial (from Latin esculus: oak, or scoria: slag)
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part II: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/junio_07/21062007_01.asp); Lorenzo Arribas (CVC Rinconete: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/enero_07/12012007_01.htm); Father Siguenza (16th c.); Sarmiento (18th c.); Casiano de Prado 1864

name: Robledo de Chavela
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Robledo' from Latin 'roburetum' (oak grove). 'Chavela' per the Toponomasticon Hispaniae: a compound of Basque 'Echa' (from 'aita', meaning father/chief, with initial vowel lost through apheresis) + Germanic 'Vela' (personal name). The toponym designates 'a forest as possession of a lord named Echa Vela'. Same 'aita'-derived pattern as Chamartin. Alternatives: Latin 'casa/chez' + Vela, or Arabic 'Djebel' (mountain).
named_after: Robledo de Chavela (oak grove of lord Echa Vela)
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae; Gregorio de Andres; MadridNorte24horas

name: Santa Maria de la Alameda-Peguerinos
etymology_summary: 'Santa Maria de la Alameda': named after a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary near a poplar grove ('alameda', from 'alamo' = poplar). 'Peguerinos' refers to the nearby village, from 'peguero' (pitch worker/tar maker).
named_after: Santa Maria de la Alameda (patron saint + poplar grove) + Peguerinos (from peguera: pine tar kiln)

name: Los Negrales
etymology_summary: Named after the Los Negrales residential area of Alpedrete, near Collado Villalba. 'Negrales' likely refers to dark-coloured rocks or dark vegetation in the area.
named_after: Los Negrales (negrales: type of pine, Pinus pinaster)

name: Alpedrete
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Hybrid word: Arabic article 'al-' + Romance 'pedrete' (stony place, from Latin petra: stone) with abundancial suffix. Literally 'the rocky place', referring to the abundant granite quarries. Same toponym repeated in Alpedrete de la Sierra (Guadalajara).
named_after: Alpedrete (Arabic al- + Romance pedrete: the stony place)
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae; MadridNorte24h; Ayuntamiento de Alpedrete

name: Collado Mediano
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Collado' from Latin 'collis' (hill/raised ground); for mountain villagers also meant an enclosure where shepherds kept livestock. 'Mediano' (medium/moderate) refers to the enclosure being of moderate size. The territory belonged to the Council of Segovia in the 12th century, repopulated by Segovian shepherds.
named_after: Collado Mediano (medium-sized hill enclosure for livestock)
source: Garcia Perez, Toponimia de la Sierra de Guadarrama (UPM: oa.upm.es/784/1/Toponimia_de_la_Sierra_de_Guadarrama.pdf); Ediciones La Libreria; etimologias.dechile.net/?collado; Amiaire.net

name: Los Molinos
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From the flour mills (molinos harineros) built along the Rio Guadarrama. At least three water mills processed cereals in the municipal area. A 1546 license records permission for Alvaro de Mena to establish a water mill on the Guadarrama. The mills were connected to the construction of El Escorial, which drove demand for flour.
named_after: Los Molinos (flour mills on the Rio Guadarrama)
source: Ayuntamiento de Los Molinos; Turismo Los Molinos; Wikipedia

name: Cercedilla
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Latin 'quercetum' (oak grove), through a diminutive form. 'Cercedilla' means 'little Cerceda'. Settlers from nearby Cerceda likely established a seasonal outpost here, named as a smaller version of the parent town. Paradoxically, Cercedilla is now larger than Cerceda.
named_after: Cercedilla (diminutive of Cerceda, from Latin quercetum: oak grove)

name: Puerto de Navacerrada
etymology_summary: Named after the Navacerrada mountain pass. 'Nava' is a term from at least the 8th century meaning flat land with pasture, liable to flooding, between mountains (RAE attributes Basque origin). 'Cerrada' from 'cercada' (enclosed/fenced), referring to enclosures built to prevent livestock from escaping -- first with branches, then stone walls. Founded by Segovian herders during Reconquista-era repopulation.
named_after: Puerto de Navacerrada (enclosed pasture plain mountain pass)

name: Cotos
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerto de los Cotos mountain pass. The name dates from 1761, when Carlos III purchased the Valsain lands and placed stone boundary markers called 'cotos' to delimit his royal property from the Carthusian Order's Pinar de los Belgas. Two restored original markers are still visible at the top of the pass. Previously called 'Puerto de El Paular' after the nearby Carthusian monastery.
named_after: Cotos (boundary markers placed by Carlos III, 1761)

name: Mirasierra-Paco de Lucia
etymology_summary: 'Mirasierra' means 'view of the mountains'. 'Paco de Lucia' honours Francisco Sanchez Gomez (1947-2014), the world-renowned flamenco guitarist who lived in this neighbourhood. Originally planned as 'Costa Brava'.

name: Ramon y Cajal
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Hospital Universitario Ramon y Cajal, which honours Santiago Ramon y Cajal (1852-1934), Nobel Prize-winning neuroscientist and 'father of modern neuroscience'.

name: Pitis
etymology_summary: Named after the Pitis area in Fuencarral-El Pardo district, a pre-existing rural place name. The area was described c.1960 as having a leafy poplar grove with a stream. The exact origin is genuinely unknown -- FilobLogos (2007) explicitly lists Pitis among names 'no se saben'. Speculative Greek 'Pitys' (pine) hypothesis has circumstantial support: the 'Arroyo de los Pinos' flows through adjacent Penagrande, and Monte de El Pardo has extensive pine forests. Alternative: personal name of a landowner, now lost. No scholarly publication has treated this toponym.
named_after: Pitis area (uncertain origin, possibly Greek pitys: pine)

name: Tres Cantos
etymology_summary: Named after the area. 'Tres Cantos' refers to three large granite boulders (cantos = stones/boulders) that were visible from a great distance in the landscape, reportedly located on the current Avenida de los Encuartes, next to which the stagecoach from Madrid to Segovia would stop. The nearby Cantoblanco has a parallel origin, named after the colour of a large stone.
source: MadridNorte24h; que.madrid; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tres_Cantos; Ayto. Tres Cantos

name: Valdebebas
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo de Valdebebas, a stream originating in the highlands of Fuencarral that crossed Las Tablas, Sanchinarro, and the Valdebebas area before emptying into the Jarama. The structure is 'Val(le)' (valley) + 'de' + 'bebas'. The meaning of 'bebas' is uncertain: possibly related to 'beber' (to drink, i.e. a watering place for livestock), a personal name, or a pre-Romance substrate term. The stream has since dried up.
named_after: Arroyo de Valdebebas (valley stream, bebas of uncertain origin)
source: valdebebas.es/blog/valdebebas-origen-nombre; Asociacion de Vecinos de Valdebebas; Wikidata Q23991457 (Arroyo de Valdebebas); Historia de Hortaleza

name: Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the Vallecas area. 'Vallecas' etymology debated: possibly from Latin 'vallis' + Arab name 'Kas' (Valley of Kas), or from 'Vallis Egas'. First documented in 1202. Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950.
source: Fuero de Madrid 1202 (cervantesvirtual.com/obra-visor/memoria-sobre-el-fuero-de-madrid-del-ano-1202--0/html/fefd3dce-82b1-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_2.htm); diccet.com/2021/01/09/vallecas; vallecas.com/la-historia-de-vallecas-desde-1202-hasta-1950; Federico Corriente (Arabic theory)

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the Vicalvaro district. 'Vicalvaro' from Arabic 'Vicus Albari' (village of Albaro) or possibly 'vicus alvarus' (white village). Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1951. Famous for the 'Vicalvarada' (1854), a military uprising.

name: Villaverde Bajo
etymology_summary: Named after the Villaverde Bajo neighbourhood. 'Villaverde' = 'green village' from Latin 'villa viridis'. 'Bajo' = 'lower'. Villaverde was independent until annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: Villaverde Alto
etymology_summary: Named after Villaverde Alto, the historic centre of the former municipality. 'Villaverde' = 'green village'. 'Alto' = 'upper/high'. Major railway junction point.

name: Universidad P. Comillas
etymology_summary: Named after the Universidad Pontificia Comillas campus. Founded 1890 in Comillas (Cantabria) by the 1st Marquis of Comillas, Antonio Lopez y Lopez. Moved to Madrid in 1960s. 'Comillas' from Latin 'cumella' (little hilltop).

name: Valdelasfuentes
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdelasfuentes area of Alcobendas. 'Valde las fuentes' = 'valley of the springs/fountains'. Describes the historically water-rich terrain with natural springs in this area.
named_after: Valdelasfuentes (Valle de las Fuentes: valley of the springs)

name: Zarzaquemada
etymology_summary: Named after the Zarzaquemada neighbourhood in Leganes. A transparent compound of 'zarza' (bramble/blackberry bush, from a pre-Roman root) + 'quemada' (burned, from Latin cremare). Literally 'burned bramble patch', indicating land cleared by slash-and-burn agriculture ('roza y quema'). At least 32 Spanish localities have zarza-derived names.
source: RAE (dle.rae.es/zarza); Rozas en la Peninsula Iberica (dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/1098569.pdf); CVC Rinconete; Secretos de Leganes; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarzaquemada

name: Villalba
etymology_summary: Named after Collado Villalba municipality. 'Collado' = mountain pass; 'Villalba' from Latin 'villa alba' (white village/estate). Major railway junction where lines to Segovia, Avila, and the Sierra diverge.

name: Las Zorreras
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Zorreras area near El Escorial. 'Zorreras' derives from 'zorra' (fox), meaning 'place of foxes'. References the historically abundant fox population in the wooded Sierra foothills.
named_after: Las Zorreras (fox dens, from zorra: fox)

name: Zarzalejo
etymology_summary: Named after the Zarzalejo municipality. 'Zarzalejo' is a diminutive of 'zarzal' (bramble patch), from 'zarza' (bramble/blackberry bush). Literally 'small bramble patch'. Similar formation to other phytonymic toponyms like Moraleja, Carrascalejo.

name: Pinar de Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after a pine grove ('pinar') near the Chamartin area. 'Chamartin' etymology debated: possibly Basque 'ecta-Martin' (village of captain Martin) or French 'Chez Martin'. Interchange with Metro lines 1 and 4.
named_after: Pinar de Chamartin (pine grove near Chamartin area)

name: Fuente de la Mora
etymology_summary: Named after the old Camino Fuente de la Mora. 'Fuente' = spring; 'Mora' may derive from pre-Roman 'mor-' (stones). Shared with Cercanias C-1. Originally planned as 'Manoteras'.
named_after: Fuente de la Mora (spring, from pre-Roman mor-: stones)
source: Garcia Sanchez CVC Rinconete Part IV (cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/enero_08/28012008_01.htm); comunidad.madrid/cultura/patrimonio-cultural/yacimiento-arqueologico-fuente-mora

name: Virgen del Cortijo
etymology_summary: Named after the Virgen del Cortijo neighbourhood (1966 development). The name refers to a devotion to the Virgin Mary associated with a local farmstead ('cortijo').
named_after: Virgen del Cortijo neighbourhood (Virgin Mary of the farmstead)

name: Antonio Saura
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Antonio Saura Atares (1930-1998), a major Spanish painter of the post-war period. Co-founder of the El Paso group (1957). Known for expressionist abstract works in black and grey tones.

name: Alvarez de Villaamil
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Jenaro Perez Villaamil y Duguet (1807-1854), the great Spanish romantic landscape painter. He introduced landscape genre painting in Spain and created 'Espana artistica y monumental'.

name: Blasco Ibanez
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Vicente Blasco Ibanez (1867-1928), Valencian novelist, journalist, and politician. Author of 'Los cuatro jinetes del Apocalipsis' and 'Sangre y arena', both adapted by Hollywood.

name: Maria Tudor
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Mary Tudor / Maria I of England (1516-1558). First queen regnant of England. Wife of Felipe II of Spain. Daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon (daughter of the Reyes Catolicos).

name: Palas de Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the street, which references Palas de Rei, a municipality in Lugo (Galicia) on the Camino de Santiago. From Latin 'Palatium Regis' (Palace of the King), linked to the Visigothic King Witiza (702-710).

name: Las Tablas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Tablas PAU (new urban development, built early 2000s). 'Tablas' means 'boards/planks' but in agricultural context refers to flat, rectangular land plots.
named_after: Las Tablas neighbourhood (tablas: flat terrain plots)

name: Colonia Jardin
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Colonia Jardin' (garden colony), a planned neighbourhood inspired by the English Garden City movement of Ebenezer Howard and the Linear City of Arturo Soria. These 'colonias' emerged around 1915-1924. Interchange with Metro line 10.
named_after: Colonia Jardin (garden city neighbourhood, early 20th-century urban planning model)

name: Prado de la Vega
etymology_summary: Named after the local area. 'Prado' means 'meadow'; 'de la Vega' means 'of the fertile plain'. Describes the former agricultural landscape of the area.
named_after: Prado de la Vega (meadow of the fertile plain)

name: Colonia de los Angeles
etymology_summary: Named after the residential colony 'Colonia de los Angeles' (Colony of the Angels), a planned suburban development in Pozuelo de Alarcon.
named_after: Colonia de los Angeles (neighbourhood near Cerro de los Angeles)

name: Prado del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the Prado del Rey area. 'Prado del Rey' means 'the King's Meadow' (from Latin pratum: meadow), indicating a royal meadow or pasture belonging to the Crown. The area was historically part of royal hunting grounds. The Arroyo Prado del Rey still flows through the area. The site later became the headquarters of RTVE (state television) from 1964, making 'Prado del Rey' synonymous with Spanish public broadcasting.
named_after: Prado del Rey (the King's Meadow, royal pastureland)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prado_del_Rey; Mesa del Arbol de Carabanchel; La Cerca

name: Somosaguas Sur
etymology_summary: Named after the Somosaguas area in Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Somosaguas' is a compound of 'somo' (from Latin summum: the highest part, elevated area) + 'aguas' (waters), referring to elevated terrain with water sources. The area historically had ferruginous springs. The hamlet of San Juan de Somosaguas was depopulated during the fratricidal wars between Pedro I and Enrique II (14th century).
named_after: Somosaguas (elevated terrain with springs, from Latin summum + aguas)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somosaguas; El Correo de Pozuelo; Grupo Abrasador

name: Somosaguas Centro
etymology_summary: Named after central Somosaguas. See Somosaguas Sur for etymology. The area is known for luxury residential urbanizations established from the mid-20th century.
named_after: Somosaguas (elevated terrain with springs, from Latin summum + aguas)

name: Pozuelo Oeste
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the western part of Pozuelo de Alarcon. See Cercanias Pozuelo entry for municipality etymology.
named_after: Pozuelo de Alarcon west (Latin puteolu: small well/spring)

name: Belgica
etymology_summary: Named after the street Calle Belgica (Belgium). Part of a European country-themed street naming pattern in this area of Pozuelo de Alarcon, reflecting European integration themes.

name: Dos Castillas
etymology_summary: Named after the Via de las Dos Castillas street. 'Dos Castillas' (Two Castiles) refers to the historical kingdoms of Castilla la Vieja and Castilla la Nueva, reflecting the area's location within the Castilian heartland.
named_after: Calle Dos Castillas (Two Castiles: Castile and Leon + Castile-La Mancha)

name: Campus de Somosaguas
etymology_summary: Named after the Complutense University campus at Somosaguas, which houses the Faculty of Political Sciences, Economics, Psychology, and Social Work.

name: Avenida de Europa
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Europa (Avenue of Europe), a major urban road through Pozuelo de Alarcon. Reflects European-themed naming in the area's modern urban developments from the 1980s-90s.

name: Berna
etymology_summary: Named after the street Calle Berna (Bern), the capital of Switzerland. Part of the European capitals/countries street naming theme in this area of Pozuelo de Alarcon.

name: Estacion de Aravaca
etymology_summary: Terminal station connecting to Cercanias. Named after the Aravaca district, of possible Celtic origin. Documented since Alfonso VIII's fuero (1222). Annexed to Madrid 1951.

name: Ciudad de la Imagen
etymology_summary: Named after the Ciudad de la Imagen (City of the Image) business park, a complex specializing in audiovisual industries. Home to Telemadrid, ECAM, Filmoteca Espanola, and many production companies.
named_after: Ciudad de la Imagen (audiovisual business park in Pozuelo)

name: Jose Isbert
etymology_summary: Named after Jose Ysbert Alvarruiz 'Pepe Isbert' (1886-1966), legendary Spanish actor. Star of classics like 'Bienvenido Mister Marshall' and 'El verdugo'. Station located near the Filmoteca Nacional in Ciudad de la Imagen.

name: Ciudad del Cine
etymology_summary: Named for its location near the Kinepolis multiplex cinema in the Ciudad de la Imagen area. 'Ciudad del Cine' = 'City of Cinema', reflecting the audiovisual theme of the development.
named_after: Ciudad del Cine (Cinema City, Boadilla del Monte film facilities area)

name: Cocheras
etymology_summary: Named after the Metro Ligero vehicle depot ('cocheras' = depots/garages) located at this station.
named_after: Cocheras (tram/light rail depot and maintenance facility)

name: Retamares
etymology_summary: Named after the Retamares area. From 'retama' (broom plant, Arabic 'ratama') + collective suffix '-es'. 'Place of broom bushes'. The area also hosts the Spanish Ministry of Defence's Estado Mayor de la Defensa.
named_after: Retamares (retamar: place of broom plants, Retama sphaerocarpa)

name: Monteprincipe
etymology_summary: Named after the Monte Principe residential urbanization, developed in the 1960s-70s on former parkland purchased for housing. The CEU San Pablo University also has a campus here.
named_after: Monteprincipe (residential development, CEU San Pablo University campus)

name: Ventorro del Cano
etymology_summary: Named after the Ventorro del Cano area in Alcorcon. 'Ventorro' is a diminutive of 'venta' (inn/tavern from Latin vendita), a small roadside establishment for travelers. 'Del Cano' is the surname of the innkeeper. Historically a stopping point (parada de postas) on the old Camino de Extremadura, documented as existing until at least 1828.
named_after: Ventorro del Cano (Cano's roadside inn on the Camino de Extremadura)

name: Prado del Espino
etymology_summary: Named after the Prado del Espino business park and area. 'Prado' = meadow; 'del Espino' = of the hawthorn/thornbush. Describes a historical meadow with hawthorn vegetation.
named_after: Prado del Espino (meadow of the hawthorn, from Latin pratum + spinus)

name: Cantabria
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Cantabria street. Cantabria is a northern Spanish region. The street follows a theme of Spanish regions/geography names in the Boadilla area.

name: Ferial de Boadilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Boadilla fairground area ('ferial' = fairground/exhibition site). 'De Boadilla' specifies the municipality.
named_after: Ferial de Boadilla (fairground/exhibition area of Boadilla del Monte)

name: Boadilla Centro
etymology_summary: Named for its central location in Boadilla del Monte. The municipality name derives from 'Bobadilla', diminutive of 'Bobada' = 'place for grazing/passage of oxen' (from Latin 'bos/bovis').

name: Nuevo Mundo
etymology_summary: Named after a street in Boadilla. 'Nuevo Mundo' = 'New World'. References the Age of Discovery and the Americas, following a historical/geographic naming theme in the development.
named_after: Calle Nuevo Mundo (New World, Americas reference in Boadilla del Monte)

name: Siglo XXI
etymology_summary: Named after the street Calle Siglo XXI ('21st Century Street'). Reflects the modern, forward-looking character of this new residential development in Boadilla.
named_after: Siglo XXI development (21st Century, modern residential area in Boadilla)

name: Infante Don Luis
etymology_summary: Named after the Infante Luis Antonio de Borbon y Farnesio (1727-1785), youngest son of King Felipe V and brother of Carlos III. He acquired the lordship of Boadilla in 1761 and commissioned the neoclassical palace (1763-1765) designed by Ventura Rodriguez.
named_after: Luis Antonio de Borbon y Farnesio

name: Puerta de Boadilla
etymology_summary: Terminal station. 'Puerta de Boadilla' = 'Gateway to Boadilla del Monte'. Serves as the main entrance point to the municipality from the Metro Ligero network.

name: Plaza de Toros
etymology_summary: Named after the Parla bullring. 'Plaza de toros' (bullring) is a transparent compound: the station serves the area near Parla's bullring.

name: Julio Romero de Torres
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Julio Romero de Torres (1874-1930), Spanish painter from Cordoba known for deeply Spanish symbolist art. Professor at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando.

name: La Ballena
etymology_summary: Named after the La Ballena neighbourhood in Parla. The name derives from a popular legend: a large natural lagoon existed in northern Parla (now the 'La Laguna' neighbourhood), and a muleteer threw his 'albarda' (pack saddle) into the water, where it floated resembling a whale's back. Residents of Getafe came to 'fish the whale'. A folk copla mocks this event. The Parque de la Ballena (built 2000) features a giant metal whale tail sculpture. The whale has become one of Parla's municipal symbols.
named_after: La Ballena (folk legend of whale sighting in Parla's lagoon)
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Ballena_(Parla); Raul Cordero 'La ciudad de la ballena'; esculturayarte.com

name: Parla Centro-Bulevar Norte
etymology_summary: 'Parla Centro' indicates the town centre location. 'Bulevar Norte' refers to the northern boulevard. The municipality name has debated etymology: Roman anthroponym 'Parilus', Latin 'parabola' (speech), or folk legend of a mute woman who began to 'parlar'.
named_after: Parla town centre + Bulevar Norte (northern boulevard)

name: Iglesia Centro
etymology_summary: Named for its proximity to the central parish church ('iglesia') of Parla, the Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion.
named_after: Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Asuncion (Parla parish church)

name: Bulevar Sur-Miguel Angel Blanco
etymology_summary: 'Bulevar Sur' = Southern Boulevard. 'Miguel Angel Blanco' (1968-1997) was a PP councillor in Ermua (Basque Country) kidnapped and murdered by ETA. Streets across Spain were named in his honour as a symbol of resistance against terrorism.

name: Reyes Catolicos
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring the Reyes Catolicos (Catholic Monarchs): Queen Isabel I of Castile (1451-1504) and King Fernando II of Aragon (1452-1516), who unified Spain and sponsored Columbus's voyage.

name: Isabel II
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Queen Isabel II of Spain (1830-1904), who reigned 1833-1868. Under her reign, major railway construction was undertaken in Spain including the Madrid-Aranjuez line.

name: Parque Parla Este
etymology_summary: Named after the park ('parque') in the eastern ('este') part of Parla.
named_after: Parque Parla Este (eastern park of Parla)

name: Avenida Sistema Solar
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida del Sistema Solar (Solar System Avenue). Part of an astronomy/space-themed street naming pattern in the Parla Este new development, with streets named after planets and celestial features.
named_after: Avenida del Sistema Solar (Solar System Avenue, astronomical theme in Parla Este)

name: Tierra
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Tierra (Earth Street). Part of the solar system/astronomy naming theme in the Parla Este development. Dual station (serves both directions of circular line).
named_after: Planet Earth (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvia)

name: Venus
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Venus (Venus Street), referencing the planet. Part of the solar system naming theme. Dual station.
named_after: Planet Venus (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvia)

name: Estrella Polar
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Estrella Polar (Polaris/North Star Street). Part of the astronomical naming theme. Dual station.
named_after: Polaris / North Star (astronomical theme in Parla Este Tranvia)

name: Jaime I
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Jaime I. Jaime I 'el Conquistador' (1208-1276) was King of Aragon who conquered the Balearic Islands, Valencia, and Murcia. Dual station.

name: Poligono Industrial Ciudad de Parla
etymology_summary: Named after Parla's main industrial park ('poligono industrial'). The term refers to the planned industrial zone of the municipality.
named_after: Poligono Industrial Ciudad de Parla (Parla industrial estate)

name: Centro
etymology_summary: Self-explanatory: the historic centre of Madrid, the original core around the Puerta del Sol and Plaza Mayor.

name: Arganzuela
etymology_summary: From 'Arganduela' meaning 'Pequena Arganda' (little Arganda). Settlers from Arganda del Rey established themselves on the south bank of the Manzanares river.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: From the Palacio del Buen Retiro (1633), built by Felipe IV as a royal retreat. The word 'retiro' means retreat/rest. Origin traces to the San Jeronimo el Real monastery where monarchs retired during Lent and mourning periods.

name: Salamanca
etymology_summary: Named after Jose de Salamanca y Mayol (1811-1883), Marquis of Salamanca, politician, financier, and real estate developer who planned and built the neighbourhood in the mid-19th century.

name: Chamartin
etymology_summary: Former independent municipality annexed in 1948. From Basque origin, per Menendez Pidal (1951). The documented medieval form 'Echamartin' (1247) contains the Castilian evolution of Basque 'aita' (father/chief), appearing in documents as 'ecta/echa'. Thus: Echa-Martin > Chamartin = 'the estate of chief Martin'. Same pattern as Chaherrero (Avila) and Robledo de Chavela.
source: Menendez Pidal 1951; documented form 'Echamartin' 1247; CVC Rinconete; Garcia Sanchez 2010

name: Tetuan
etymology_summary: Named 'Tetuan de las Victorias' after Spanish troops returning from victory at Tetouan (Morocco) in the African War of 1860. The soldiers camped in this area upon their return, and the settlement that grew around it took the name.

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: Disputed etymology. The most probable link is via Queen Barbara de Braganza, who founded the Royal Salesas Convent (c.1748) with nuns from Chambery/Annecy in Savoy; the toponym first appears on Chalmandrier's 1761 map. Alternative: Luisa Gabriela de Saboya (wife of Felipe V). The Napoleonic regiment theory is refuted by the 1761 map predating Napoleon. Other theories: French regiment during War of Independence; Celtic origin.
source: Pedro de Repide; Chalmandrier map 1761; Secretos de Madrid; Caridad Arias 2004; Chamberi30dias; Ayuntamiento de Madrid 'Historia de Chamberi'

name: Fuencarral-El Pardo
etymology_summary: Compound name. Fuencarral: from 'Fuente Carral' -- a spring (fuente) where carts (carros) stopped and animals drank on the old road to Alcobendas. The stopping place for carts was called a 'carra'. El Pardo: from the brownish/dark ('pardo') colour of the landscape of the royal hunting estate.
source: El Rincon de Mayrit; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuencarral; Historias Matritenses; Vena Madrid

name: Moncloa-Aravaca
etymology_summary: Compound name. Moncloa: from the Palacio de la Moncloa, possibly from 'Mons Clovis' (Latin). Now the official residence of the Prime Minister. Aravaca: Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004) argues for Celtic origin, with the root *ara- meaning 'water'. First documented 1427; appears in Alfonso VIII's 1222 fuero.

name: Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist scholar who was Latin tutor and advisor to Queen Isabel la Catolica. She founded the Hospital de la Latina in this area.

name: Carabanchel
etymology_summary: Former independent municipalities (Alto and Bajo) annexed in 1948. The most accepted etymology traces it to the pre-Roman/Indo-European root *kar-/*karav- meaning 'stone' (per Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953), describing 'stony ground'. Menendez Pidal links it to Garabandal (Cantabria) as a variant. The earliest documented form is 'Caravangiel/Caravanchel' (1 January 1181, original parchment in Archivo de la Catedral de Toledo); 'Carauanchiel' appears in 1264. Alternatives: Arabic 'carab' (cultivable land, per Oliver Asin); 'garbanzal' (chickpea field); Illyrian anthroponym Caravantius with diminutive Carabancilius (per Caridad Arias 2004).
source: Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004: dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); Oliver Asin; Archivo Catedral de Toledo (1181 doc)

name: Usera
etymology_summary: Named after Colonel Marcelo Usera, who married the daughter of 'Tio Sordillo', a farmer whose lands he proposed to develop into housing plots (1925-1930).

name: Puente de Vallecas
etymology_summary: 'Vallecas' from 'Valle de Cas' (oak valley), documented as 'Balecas' in the 1202 Fuero de Madrid. 'Puente' (bridge) refers to a bridge over the Abroigal stream that connected the area to Madrid proper.

name: Moratalaz
etymology_summary: Hybrid pre-Arabic/Arabic toponym per Teres Sadaba (CSIC 1986): 'Morat' (pre-Arabic/Visigothic: elevated place/height) + 'Alfaz' (Arabic: sown/cultivated field) = 'cultivated field on a height'. First documented as 'Morat Alfaz' in 1206 in a property deed benefiting the Order of Calatrava. Madrid-specific first mention: 1425. Alternative: from vulgar Latin *Muratella* (from *murus*: wall).

name: Ciudad Lineal
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata's (1844-1920) revolutionary 'Ciudad Lineal' (linear city) urban planning concept, conceived 1882/1886 and built 1892-1911. A narrow city stretching along a single transportation axis, with the boulevard Calle de Arturo Soria as its spine.

name: Hortaleza
etymology_summary: Former independent village annexed to Madrid in 1950. First documented 1361. Disputed etymology: (1) Latin 'hortus' (garden/orchard) -- most commonly cited but weakened by Felipe II's 1579 Relaciones noting main crops were cereals, not vegetables; (2) Latin 'Orta Lucis' (sunrise) -- proposed by Vicente Muzas in La Ciudad Lineal no. 323 (1907), supported by the historical spelling 'Ortaleza' without H until mid-19th century; (3) Corruption of 'fortaleza' (fortress) -- no archaeological remains found.
source: Relaciones topograficas Felipe II 1579; Muzas 1907 (La Ciudad Lineal no. 323); periodicohortaleza.org/la-fabula-del-nombre-de-hortaleza; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hortaleza_(municipio)

name: Villaverde
etymology_summary: 'Villa verde' = green village/town, from Latin 'villa viridis'. A descriptive name referring to the verdant landscape of this former independent municipality south of Madrid. Annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: Villa de Vallecas
etymology_summary: 'Vallecas' etymology debated: from Latin 'vallis' + Arab personal name 'Kas', or from 'Vallis Egas'. 'Villa' denotes its former status as an independent municipality. First documented in 1202 in the Fuero de Madrid as 'Balecas'. Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: From 'Vico Alvaro' = Alvaro's village/settlement. A pre-medieval personal name attached to the Latin 'vicus' (village). Former independent municipality annexed in 1951. Famous for the 'Vicalvarada' or Pronunciamiento de Vicalvaro (1854), a military uprising led by General O'Donnell.

name: San Blas-Canillejas
etymology_summary: Compound name. San Blas: patron saint (Saint Blaise, 4th-century Armenian bishop and martyr) of the original parish church. Canillejas: ancient municipality documented from the 13th century, annexed in 1949. Canillejas served as an agricultural settlement for over six centuries.

name: Barajas
etymology_summary: Former independent municipality annexed in 1949. Etymology debated: (1) Bar Axa theory: Philip II's 1575 Relaciones topograficas record 'en tiempo que los moros fue senor de este pueblo un moro llamado Baraja hijo de una mora llamada Aja'. Covarrubias (Tesoro 1611) supports this. (2) Latin *varalia* (fence of crossbars) per Nieto Ballester (1997). (3) Latin *uaralia* (quarrel/litigation) per Gutierre Tibon. (4) Pre-Roman toponym per Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007).
source: Philip II Relaciones topograficas 1575; Covarrubias, Tesoro de la lengua 1611; Nieto Ballester 1997; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007); cvc.cervantes.es/foros/leer_asunto1.asp?vCodigo=45869

name: Malasana
etymology_summary: Named after Manuela Malasana (1791-1808), a young seamstress killed resisting Napoleon's troops during the May 2, 1808 uprising. The neighbourhood was formerly called 'Barrio de las Maravillas' (after the Virgen de las Maravillas convent). The name Malasana became popular during the 1980s Movida cultural movement.

name: Lavapies
etymology_summary: Disputed etymology: (1) From a fountain where Jews washed their feet ('lava pies') before entering the synagogue in the nearby Jewish quarter; (2) From the muddy Manzanares river waters that dirtied feet. The Jewish quarter theory is most widely cited but debated by historians.

name: Chueca
etymology_summary: Named after composer Federico Chueca (1846-1908), master of the genero chico zarzuela (Spanish light opera). The plaza was named after him; the barrio adopted the name. Since the 1990s it has become Madrid's main LGBTQ+ neighbourhood.

name: Barrio de las Letras
etymology_summary: Named for the cluster of Golden Age (Siglo de Oro) writers who lived there in the 16th-17th centuries: Miguel de Cervantes, Lope de Vega, Francisco de Quevedo, Luis de Gongora. Also known as Huertas.

name: Salamanca
etymology_summary: Named after Jose de Salamanca y Mayol (1811-1883), Marquis of Salamanca, the financier who developed and built this upscale neighbourhood in the mid-19th century.

name: Los Austrias
etymology_summary: Named after the House of Austria (Habsburg dynasty) that ruled Spain from 1516 (Charles I) to 1700 (Charles II). This is the oldest part of Madrid, developed during Habsburg rule, including the Plaza Mayor (1619) and surrounding streets.

name: Prosperidad
etymology_summary: Named after Prospero Soynard, a Frenchman who bought land north of Madrid in 1862 and subdivided it for development. The settlement that grew was called 'Prosperidad' after his first name.

name: Delicias
etymology_summary: From 'las delicias del rio' (the delights of the river). The Paseo de las Delicias was created mid-18th century under Fernando VI as an extension of the Paseo del Prado heading south toward the Manzanares. The nearby Delicias railway station (1880) is now the Railway Museum.

name: Leganitos
etymology_summary: From Arabic 'algannet' meaning 'the orchards' or 'the gardens'. Refers to the agricultural land that existed in this area before urbanization. The Calle de los Leganitos preserves the name.

name: Vallecas
etymology_summary: From 'Valle de Cas' (oak valley), documented as 'Balecas' in the 1202 Fuero de Madrid. One of the oldest documented place names in the Madrid area.

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: See district entry. Disputed etymology linked to Chambery in Savoy, France. Multiple theories involving French/Savoyard connections.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: Named after the Buen Retiro Palace (1633), built as a royal retreat for Felipe IV by the Count-Duke of Olivares. 'Retiro' means retreat. Origin traces to the San Jeronimo el Real monastery where monarchs retired during Lent and mourning periods. Opened to the public in 1868. UNESCO World Heritage since 2021.

name: Sol
etymology_summary: From the Puerta del Sol, one of Madrid's medieval fortress gates. The gate may have had a sun carved on it, or it faced east toward the sunrise. First documented during the 1520-1522 Comuneros revolt.

name: La Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist scholar famous for her Latin expertise, who served as tutor and advisor to Queen Isabel la Catolica. She founded the Hospital de la Latina nearby.

name: Embajadores
etymology_summary: From 'embajadores' (ambassadors). During the reign of King Juan II (15th century), foreign ambassadors fled a plague outbreak in Madrid and took refuge outside the city walls in this area. The street leading to their encampment became known as Calle de Embajadores.

name: Opera
etymology_summary: Named after the Teatro Real (Royal Opera House) inaugurated in 1850 on the Plaza de Oriente. The surrounding area and the Metro station took the name.

name: Arguelles
etymology_summary: Named after Agustin de Arguelles (1776-1844), a liberal lawyer and politician who participated in the Cortes of Cadiz and helped draft the 1812 Constitution. Known as 'El Divino' for his oratory.

name: Moncloa
etymology_summary: From the Palacio de la Moncloa, which takes its name from the Condesa de Moncloa who owned the estate. Now the official residence of the President of the Government of Spain. The name may derive from 'Mons Clovis' (Latin for Mount of Clovis), referencing the Frankish king.

name: Atocha
etymology_summary: From the pre-Roman word *taucia meaning 'mata/matorral' (thicket/shrubland). 'Atocha' is a synonym for esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) per the RAE. Corominas traces it through Mozarabic *attawca* back to pre-Roman *taucia. First documented in the Fuero de Madrid (1202) as 'Prato de Toia'. Site of the Basilica de Nuestra Senora de Atocha and Spain's first railway terminus (1851).
source: CVC Cervantes; Corominas; Fuero de Madrid 1202; eldiario.es

name: Callao
etymology_summary: Named in tribute to the 1866 naval Battle of Callao, where the Spanish fleet attacked the Peruvian port of Callao. The plaza was named to commemorate the battle.

name: Puerta del Sol
etymology_summary: One of Madrid's original medieval fortress gates. The gate may have had a sun ('sol') carved on it, or it faced east toward the sunrise. First documented during the 1520-22 Comuneros revolt. Now considered the geographic centre of Spain (Km 0).
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerta_del_Sol; Renfe Blog (renfe.com); Secretos de Madrid

name: Plaza Mayor
etymology_summary: 'Main Square' -- built 1617-1619 under Felipe III by architect Juan Gomez de Mora. Originally called 'Plaza del Arrabal' (square of the outskirts) when it was a marketplace outside the medieval walls.

name: Plaza de Espana
etymology_summary: Named to honour Spain. Features the Cervantes monument (1929) with statues of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza.

name: Plaza de Cibeles
etymology_summary: Named after the Fuente de Cibeles (1782), a fountain depicting the Roman goddess Cybele riding a chariot pulled by lions. Designed by Ventura Rodriguez.

name: Plaza de Neptuno
etymology_summary: Named after the Fuente de Neptuno (1786), depicting the Roman god Neptune on a chariot pulled by sea horses. Now officially 'Plaza de Canovas del Castillo'.
previous_names: Plaza de Canovas del Castillo (official name)

name: Plaza de Oriente
etymology_summary: Named for its location to the east ('oriente') of the Royal Palace. Paradoxically, it is west of the city centre -- the name refers to the palace's orientation.

name: Parque del Retiro
etymology_summary: Originally the gardens of the Buen Retiro Palace (1633), built as a royal retreat for Felipe IV. 'Retiro' means retreat. Opened to the public in 1868 after the fall of Isabel II. UNESCO World Heritage since 2021.

name: Casa de Campo
etymology_summary: Originally a royal hunting estate ('casa de campo' = country house) acquired by Felipe II in 1562. Opened to the public during the Second Republic (1931). At 1,722 hectares, it is the largest public park in Madrid.

name: Parque del Oeste
etymology_summary: 'Western Park' -- created in 1906 by landscape architect Cecilio Rodriguez on former military land on the western edge of the city. Contains the Templo de Debod.

name: Plaza de Castilla
etymology_summary: Named to honour the historical region of Castilla (Castile). Features the Torres Kio/Puerta de Europa inclined towers.

name: Puerta de Alcala
etymology_summary: Monumental gate built 1769-1778 by architect Francesco Sabatini, commissioned by King Carlos III. Named because it stands on the road to Alcala de Henares. One of Madrid's most iconic landmarks.

name: Puerta de Toledo
etymology_summary: Built 1813-1827, originally planned to honour Napoleon's brother Joseph Bonaparte, but repurposed as a triumphal arch for King Fernando VII. Named for its position on the road to Toledo.

name: Parque de la Dehesa de la Villa
etymology_summary: 'Dehesa' means a common pasture/woodland. This was communal grazing land ('dehesa') belonging to the 'villa' (town) of Madrid since medieval times.

name: Madrid Rio
etymology_summary: Named for its location along the Manzanares River ('rio'). Created 2006-2011 by burying the M-30 motorway, transforming the riverbank into a linear park.

name: Calle de Alcala
etymology_summary: Named as the main road leading to Alcala de Henares, the ancient Roman city of Complutum east of Madrid. One of the longest and oldest streets in Madrid.

name: Gran Via
etymology_summary: 'Great Way' -- Madrid's grand east-west boulevard, built 1910-1929 by demolishing hundreds of old buildings to create a modern commercial thoroughfare. Project proposed by Carlos Velasco in 1886.

name: Calle de Preciados
etymology_summary: Named after the Preciado family, landowners who owned property along this street since medieval times. The name was already documented in the 15th century.

name: Calle del Arenal
etymology_summary: From 'arenal' (sandy ground). The street was built over a sandy terrain/streambed. A common descriptive name for areas with sandy soil.

name: Calle de los Cuchilleros
etymology_summary: Named after the knife-makers ('cuchilleros') whose workshops lined this street near the Plaza Mayor. One of the classic trade-guild street names of medieval Madrid.

name: Calle de Esparteros
etymology_summary: Named after the esparto grass weavers ('esparteros') who had their workshops here, making baskets, mats, and sandals from esparto fiber.

name: Calle de Latoneros
etymology_summary: Named after the brass/tin workers ('latoneros') who operated workshops in this area near the Plaza Mayor.

name: Calle de Cabestreros
etymology_summary: Named after the rope/halter makers ('cabestreros') who produced cabestros (halters/lead ropes) for livestock. Part of the medieval guild street naming pattern.

name: Calle de Toledo
etymology_summary: Named as the ancient road leading south from Madrid to Toledo, the former capital of Castile. One of the oldest documented street names in Madrid.

name: Calle de Segovia
etymology_summary: Named as the road leading northwest to Segovia. Follows the route of an ancient path that descended from the Moorish alcazar toward the Manzanares river.

name: Calle de Hortaleza
etymology_summary: Named as the road leading north to the village of Hortaleza (now a district of Madrid). The name Hortaleza itself has disputed etymology (orchards or sunrise).

name: Calle de Fuencarral
etymology_summary: Named as the road leading north to the village of Fuencarral ('Fuente del Carral' -- a water source). Now a major shopping street.

name: Paseo del Prado
etymology_summary: 'Prado' means meadow (from Latin pratum). Named after the meadow that existed along the eastern edge of the old city. The paseo (promenade) was developed in the 18th century under Carlos III. Part of the UNESCO-listed 'Landscape of Light' (2021).

name: Paseo de la Castellana
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Paseo Nuevo de las Delicias de la Princesa' and later 'Paseo de la Fuente Castellana', referring to a fountain with water from a 'castellana' (castle-related source). Madrid's main north-south artery.

name: Calle de Arturo Soria
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata (1844-1920), visionary urbanist who designed the Ciudad Lineal (Linear City) concept, a pioneering model of urban planning built 1892-1911. This 15km boulevard was the spine of his utopian urban plan.

name: Calle Mayor
etymology_summary: 'Main Street' -- one of the oldest streets in Madrid, following the route from the Moorish alcazar (now Royal Palace) eastward. Historically the most important commercial and ceremonial route.

name: Calle de la Princesa
etymology_summary: Named after Princess Isabel (later Isabel II, 1830-1904), when she was still princess. One of the main arteries connecting the city center to the western outskirts.

name: Calle de Serrano
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Serrano y Dominguez (1810-1885), Duke of la Torre, military leader and regent of Spain (1869-1871) during the Revolutionary Sexennium. The street was named after the 1868 revolution.

name: Calle de Velazquez
etymology_summary: Named after Diego Velazquez (1599-1660), the great painter of the Spanish Golden Age, court painter to Felipe IV. Author of 'Las Meninas'.

name: Calle de Cervantes
etymology_summary: Named after Miguel de Cervantes (1547-1616), author of Don Quixote, who lived and died on this street (then called Calle de Francos). The house where he died was at #2.

name: Calle de Lope de Vega
etymology_summary: Named after Lope de Vega (1562-1635), the prolific Golden Age playwright ('Monster of Nature'). His house at #11 is now a museum.

name: Calle de Quevedo
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco de Quevedo (1580-1645), poet and prose writer of the Spanish Golden Age, famous for his picaresque novel 'El Buscon'.

name: Calle del Limon
etymology_summary: Named after a lemon tree ('limon') that grew at this location. One of many Madrid streets named after trees or plants.

name: Calle del Almendro
etymology_summary: Named after an almond tree ('almendro') that grew in the area. Part of the traditional pattern of naming streets after local vegetation.

name: Calle de la Ruda
etymology_summary: Named after the rue plant ('ruda', Ruta graveolens), an herb used in traditional medicine and believed to ward off evil spirits.

name: Calle de la Fe
etymology_summary: 'Street of Faith' -- named after the abstract concept of faith ('fe'). Part of a cluster of streets in Lavapies named after virtues (Fe, Esperanza, Amor de Dios).

name: Calle de la Esperanza
etymology_summary: 'Street of Hope' -- named after the virtue of hope ('esperanza'). Part of the virtues cluster with Fe and Amor de Dios.

name: Calle Amor de Dios
etymology_summary: 'Love of God Street' -- named after a religious concept. Part of the virtues cluster near Lavapies. Known today as the birthplace of flamenco tablaos in Madrid.

name: Calle de Atocha
etymology_summary: Named after the atocha/esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) that grew in the area, leading to the Basilica de Nuestra Senora de Atocha.

name: Calle de la Cuesta de Santo Domingo
etymology_summary: Named after the Convento de Santo Domingo el Real, a major Dominican convent founded in 1218. 'Cuesta' refers to the hill/slope leading up to it.
named_after: Convento de Santo Domingo el Real
